A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research framework and contain readable text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices. Retained material can be matched despite extensive reformatting and appendix reorganization.

before.justification: v2 reports original vehicle-routing experiments and synthetic gradient and parameter-recovery experiments, including extensive appendix analyses.

after.justification: v3 retains those original experiments and adds multi-dimensional knapsack results in Section 5.3 and Appendix D.

M1.justification: Algorithms 1–2 and the Fenchel-Young learning framework are retained. The knapsack adaptation introduces uniform swaps and predicted-value-guided swap and flip proposals (Appendix D.1), a limited procedural addition.

E1.justification: v3 adds feature-conditioned multi-dimensional knapsack prediction with 100 items and 50 capacity constraints. This extends evaluation beyond routing and synthetic binary/top-k parameter recovery; v2's knapsack discussion only concerned implementing the top-k reference oracle.

E2.justification: The new knapsack comparison evaluates SPO+, NID, and NCE alongside PFY (Figure 4). Appendix D.4 additionally compares PFY using Gurobi versus the final local-search iterate. The routing comparator is retained, renamed from 'Perturbed inexact oracle' to 'PFY with ỹ'.

E3.justification: The knapsack experiments introduce an 80/10/10 split, 20-epoch training, 1 ms training-oracle limits, a common 50 ms evaluation solver, and a 0.1–10 ms budget sweep. Existing routing protocols remain unchanged. The new sample count is inconsistent: Section 5.3 states 2,000 instances, whereas Appendix D.2 states 5,000.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained sensitivity and initialization analyses, v3 adds comparisons of gradient variability (Figure 4) and a knapsack budget sweep with solver optimality gaps (Figure 16). Comparing against PFY using the same local-search oracle specifically examines whether advantages arise from gradient estimation rather than solver choice.

E5.justification: Figure 4 newly quantifies stochastic-gradient variability using average covariance trace over training. The routing experiments retain 50 random-seed trainings and 95% confidence intervals. No knapsack-specific run count or confidence-interval procedure is documented.

E6.justification: Figure 4 adds knapsack results, including 18.42% best test relative regret for LS-MCMC versus 31.15% for PFY, and 0.005 versus 0.198 seconds per forward/backward batch. Figure 16 shows Gurobi-based PFY overtaking LS-MCMC at 5–10 ms. Earlier plotted results and Table 3 are retained apart from equivalent rounding.

T1.justification: Propositions 1–7 and their convergence assumptions are retained. Limited mathematical changes include adding beta denominators in the routing remove-request reverse-probability derivation (v2 B.4; v3 C.5) and defining the new knapsack neighborhoods and proposals. Reordering the existing proofs does not constitute new theory.

C1.justification: The abstract and contribution list add multi-dimensional knapsack as a demonstrated application. The central claims concerning local-search MCMC layers, Fenchel-Young learning, and computational efficiency remain unchanged; binary/top-k experiments newly highlighted in the abstract already existed in v2.

C2.justification: v3 adds explicit limitations concerning access to solver internals and restriction to single-trajectory local search. It explains why population-based PC-HGS or nearly exact Gurobi-based PFY can outperform the method with more computation, and interprets the new gradient-variability and same-oracle comparisons. These substantially qualify the earlier emphasis on efficiency.

D1.justification: Appendix D adds knapsack proposal probabilities, feature and noise generation, capacity settings, label-generation budgets, MLP architecture, optimizer, and batch size. Section A.1 replaces the PyTorch-autodiff account of exact top-k gradients with references to specific dynamic-programming algorithms. The conflicting knapsack sample counts limit reproducibility.

R1.justification: v3 adds references for the new comparison methods, PyEPO, MIPaaL, knapsack problems, and two 2026 Vivier-Ardisson works. It distinguishes decision-focused learning from neural combinatorial optimization and acknowledges an existing large-neighborhood-search extension. Numerous other bibliography edits merely update publication metadata.

P1.justification: Substantial rewriting clarifies the problem setup, oracle terminology, learning interpretation, and routing formulation. Routing proposal design moves from B.4 into C.5, proofs are reordered and separated, and the conclusion gains dedicated limitations and future-work discussion.

P2.justification: The document is comprehensively retypeset, changing fonts, margins, author layout, and the size and placement of existing plots and tables. New Figures 4 and 16 display knapsack comparisons and budget analyses. The earlier plotted curves are retained.

improvement.justification: v3 strengthens empirical scrutiny beyond v2's routing application and PFY comparison, while Appendix D.4 helps distinguish solver choice from gradient-estimation effects. Explicit limitations also clarify when efficiency advantages apply. These are useful quality gains, although the conflicting knapsack sample counts in Section 5.3 and Appendix D.2 weaken reproducibility and temper the improvement.
